title: Priority 2: Revise Requirements to Recognize Learning Across Contexts
author: Michael B. Horn et al.
summary: Michael B. Horn shares the third of six Christensen Institute papers, written with Angela Jackson, Mallory Dwinal-Palisch, and Danny Curtis, that together form a state policy playbook for integrated education-to-career systems. This paper argues that the rules governing what counts as learning, for high school credit, a college degree, and a professional license, are a major barrier to career-connected pathways. It makes three recommendations: make room for work-based learning in graduation requirements, evaluate learning from across settings for college credit, and revise licensure rules to recognize it. Each is read through Business Model Theory and a Chesterton's Fence caution against rebuilding a tracked system. Indiana's graduation and diploma redesign is the extended example, with doubled elective credits, three pathways, and honors seals. The paper stresses that permission on paper is not enough without implementation support.
points: Because work-based learning usually counts only as an elective, crowded graduation requirements leave students little time to leave campus for sustained workplace experiences.
Graduation waivers help far less than policymakers assume because the extra steps discourage schools and students from using them, so work-based learning must be part of the normal path to a diploma.

Credit for prior learning policies are common, yet one national study found only 11 percent of adult students actually received such credit, which shows that permission without institutional capacity does little.
Indiana doubled elective credits, created three pathways for college, military, and employment, and redesigned the diploma with honors seals to build demand as well as supply.
The authors warn states to keep a rigorous common academic foundation so that career-connected pathways expand opportunity rather than recreate tracking.
quotes: If work-based learning is to become mainstream, it must be part of the normal path to graduation—not a special exception available only to those who navigate a waiver process.
Yet waivers help far less than most policymakers believe. The extra steps required to obtain a waiver discourage schools and students from using them.

Traditional graduation requirements can crowd out work-based learning, but they also maintain a common academic foundation designed to prepare students for college—a path that most high school graduates still pursue.
That means states should be careful not to recreate a tracked system under a more modern label.
The new requirements doubled the number of elective credits allowed, which enabled students to tailor their education to their chosen pathway and field.

A national study of institutions with credit for prior learning policies found that only 11 percent of adult students—a population especially likely to bring substantial prior learning—actually received such credit.
Permission on paper has been a necessary prerequisite to change but not enough to bring it about.
